idiom_name: Jakarta Faces navigation rules resolved by NavigationHandler.handleNavigation
implementation_notes: The Jakarta Faces platform already implements the pattern: a NavigationHandler receives the outcome string returned by an executed action together with the current view and resolves the next view from the <navigation-rule>/<navigation-case> declarations in faces-config.xml, with the flow document id giving the wizard feature explicit scopes. handleNavigation(FacesContext, fromAction, outcome) is the decision call and the default implementation must be thread-safe. What replaces the classic controller-plus-command structure is this declarative rule set plus the platform handler: actions become backing-bean methods that return outcomes and the view reference is <to-view-id>. Extend ConfigurableNavigationHandler, or register your own NavigationHandler, only when the decision needs logic that rules cannot express (permissions, dynamic view selection); if the application is not a Faces application, use Spring Web Flow or the hand-written registry variant instead.
code_sketch:
public String chooseAccount() {
    order.setAccount(cart.getSelected());
    return order.isCorporate() ? "corporateAmount" : "amountEntry";  // outcome -> rule
}

<!-- faces-config.xml
<navigation-rule>
  <from-view-id>/order/select.xhtml</from-view-id>
  <navigation-case>
    <from-outcome>amountEntry</from-outcome>
    <to-view-id>/order/amount.xhtml</to-view-id>
    <redirect/>
  </navigation-case>
</navigation-rule> -->
pitfalls: Outcomes are untyped strings: a renamed outcome that matches no rule silently redraws the current view instead of failing, so outcomes belong in constants and the rules need tests.
A custom NavigationHandler must be thread-safe and must delegate to the previous handler rather than bypass it, or every rule unrelated to your logic stops matching.
Splitting the flow between navigation rules and logic inside individual backing beans re-creates the duplication the pattern removes; the rules must stay the only description of the sequence.

variants.name: Spring Web Flow flow definition (FlowController + FlowExecutor)
variants.idiom_name: flow definition XML (view-state / action-state / decision-state) driven by FlowController
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Web Flow externalises the whole conversation: a flow definition declares view-states, action-states and decision-states, transitions are triggered by events returned from the view or from an action, and decision-states branch on evaluated expressions; FlowExecutor and FlowRegistry execute the definition behind a FlowController (Spring MVC) while flow scope keeps the model across steps and the framework enforces POST/redirect/GET and back-button protection. This replaces the classic controller with a flow definition plus the framework executor, and it is the heavier but more complete option when the wizard has real branches and must survive restarts; for a handful of screens the Faces rules or a hand-written registry are cheaper.
variants.code_sketch:
<flow xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/webflow">
  <view-state id="select" view="order/select">
    <transition on="chosen" to="amount"/>
  </view-state>
  <view-state id="amount" view="order/amount">
    <transition on="next" to="review">
      <evaluate expression="order.validate(amount)"/>
    </transition>
  </view-state>
  <decision-state id="review">
    <if test="order.needsApproval()" then="approval" else="confirm"/>
  </decision-state>
</flow>
pitfalls: Flow definitions are XML evaluated at runtime: a typo in a state id is a start-up or mid-conversation error, so flows need integration tests that walk every path.
Flow scope is conversation state kept by the framework - with session replication or a shared repository it must be serialisable, and long-lived flows need an expiry policy.

variants.name: hand-written Action objects + Map<String,Action> registry (framework-free)
variants.idiom_name: interface Action { String run(Context ctx); } + Map<String,Action> registry
variants.implementation_notes: Without Faces or Web Flow the classic form is written by hand: one Action (Command) per step implementing a small interface whose return value is the next view id, a Map<String, Action> registry consulted by a single controller method, and a Context object carrying the session state so the actions do not touch HttpServletRequest. The decisions live in that controller method - typically a switch over the current step plus the guards - and the view ids stay abstract names resolved by the view layer. This is the right shape for dependency-free servlet or Spring MVC applications and for flows that must be registered dynamically; its weakness is that registry keys and view ids are unchecked strings.
pitfalls: String keys and view ids are not checked by the compiler; keep them in constants and cover the (step, guard) matrix with tests.
An Action that reads HttpServletRequest directly welds the flow to the servlet API - pass the context abstraction instead, or the controller becomes untestable.
